## 1. What is Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)?

EDA is the process of:

- **Understanding** the structure, patterns and quirks in your dataset
- **Cleaning** the data by handling missing values, duplicates and incorrect types
- **Visualising** distributions, trends and relationships between variables
- **Generating hypotheses** or questions for further modelling and analysis

In simple terms, EDA helps you **get to know your data** before you build any model.

## 5. Exploring Missing Values

```{r missing-count}
colSums(is.na(df))                                  # missing values per column
round(100 * colMeans(is.na(df)), 1)                 # percentage missing
```

```{r missing-plot}
# Heatmap of missing values: each cell is one value, dark = missing
df |>
  mutate(row = row_number()) |>
  pivot_longer(-row, values_transform = as.character) |>
  ggplot(aes(name, row, fill = is.na(value))) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey90", "firebrick"), labels = c("present", "missing")) +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  labs(title = "Heatmap of missing values", x = "Column", y = "Row", fill = "") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

### 5.1 Example: Handling Missing Values

```{r impute}
numeric_col <- "Age"                                # TODO: change to a real column

sum(is.na(df[[numeric_col]]))                       # missing before

median_value <- median(df[[numeric_col]], na.rm = TRUE)
df[[numeric_col]] <- replace_na(df[[numeric_col]], median_value)

sum(is.na(df[[numeric_col]]))                       # should now be 0
```

## 6. Removing Duplicate Rows

```{r duplicates}
sum(duplicated(df))        # how many exact duplicate rows?

df <- distinct(df)         # keep the first occurrence of each row

sum(duplicated(df))        # should be 0
```

## 7. Univariate Analysis of Numerical Features

```{r univariate}
num_cols <- df |> select(where(is.numeric)) |> names()
num_cols

# One histogram per numerical column (faceted)
df |>
  select(all_of(num_cols)) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 25, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free") +
  labs(title = "Distributions of numerical variables", x = NULL, y = "Frequency")
```

```{r boxplots}
df |>
  select(all_of(num_cols)) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(y = value)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue") +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free") +
  labs(title = "Boxplots of numerical variables", y = NULL)
```

## 8. Outlier Detection Using the IQR Method

A value is flagged as an outlier if it lies below $Q_1 - 1.5\,\mathrm{IQR}$ or above $Q_3 + 1.5\,\mathrm{IQR}$, where $\mathrm{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1$.

```{r iqr}
count_outliers <- function(x) {
  q <- quantile(x, c(0.25, 0.75), na.rm = TRUE)
  iqr <- q[2] - q[1]
  sum(x < q[1] - 1.5 * iqr | x > q[2] + 1.5 * iqr, na.rm = TRUE)
}

df |> summarise(across(all_of(num_cols), count_outliers)) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "column", values_to = "n_outliers") |>
  arrange(desc(n_outliers))
```

## 9. Correlation and Relationships Between Numerical Features

```{r correlation}
corr_matrix <- cor(df[num_cols], use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
round(corr_matrix, 2)

as_tibble(corr_matrix, rownames = "x") |>
  pivot_longer(-x, names_to = "y", values_to = "r") |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y, fill = r)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", r)), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "steelblue", mid = "white", high = "firebrick", limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Correlation heatmap of numerical features", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

```{r pairs, eval=FALSE}
# Optional pair plot (needs install.packages("GGally")); slow on large data.
GGally::ggpairs(df[c("Age", "Fare", "SibSp", "Parch")])
```

## 10. Analysis of Categorical Features

```{r categorical}
cat_cols <- df |> select(where(is.character)) |>
  select(where(~ n_distinct(.x) <= 10)) |> names()   # skip text columns with many levels
cat_cols

df |>
  select(all_of(cat_cols)) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "category") |>
  count(variable, category) |>
  ggplot(aes(n, reorder(category, n))) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Frequency of categories", x = "Count", y = NULL)
```

> ✏️ **Student Task:** Pick one categorical feature. Which category appears most frequently? Is the distribution balanced or imbalanced? What might that imply?

## 12. Optional Extension Tasks (For Further Learning)

If you finish early, try one or more of these:

1. **Feature importance (if you have a target variable):** fit a decision tree with `rpart::rpart()` and read the variable importance (`model$variable.importance`).
2. **Compare before and after cleaning:** keep a copy of the original data frame (`df_raw <- df`) and compare distributions before and after imputation or outlier handling.
3. **Dimensionality reduction (PCA):** standardise the numerical features, run `prcomp(x, scale. = TRUE)`, and plot the first two principal components.
